# SECTION: GETTING STARTED
================================================================================

## Overview & Philosophy
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/overview

## What is Simple Relay?

**Simple Relay** is a lightweight, self-hosted reliability layer for HTTP traffic. It acts as an autonomous buffer and proxy between external services and your internal backend.

Building reliable webhook ingestion and outbound API retries usually forces engineering teams to assemble heavy distributed infrastructure: message brokers, external caching tiers, worker processes, and separate databases.

Simple Relay eliminates that operational tax: **one single binary, zero infrastructure friction, reliable HTTP delivery.**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["External Senders<br/>(Stripe, GitHub, etc.)"] -->|"HTTP POST<br/>(ACK < 2ms)"| B["Simple Relay<br/>(Persist & Retry)"]
    B -->|"Reliable Forward<br/>(At-Least-Once)"| C["Your Application<br/>(Internal APIs)"]
```

---

## The Core Pillars of Simple Relay

Simple Relay is engineered around three mission-critical guarantees:

### 1. Zero Data Loss (Persist Before ACK)
In-memory queues and background threads inside your application runtime disappear whenever processes restart, deploy, or crash. External webhook providers (such as Stripe, Shopify, or GitHub) may back off for hours or drop deliveries entirely if your server blips.

Simple Relay strictly enforces **Persist-Before-ACK**: raw incoming byte payloads and headers are flushed to durable, crash-resilient local storage *before* returning HTTP `200 OK` to the sender. Once acknowledged, delivery to your backend is guaranteed.

### 2. Ultra-Fast Inbound ACK Response Time (< 2ms)
External webhook providers impose aggressive response timeouts—often between 2 and 5 seconds. If your application attempts to execute database transactions, trigger analytics, or send emails synchronously inside the webhook handler, sudden load spikes will cause upstream timeouts. When timeouts occur, external providers flag your endpoint as failing and will automatically disable your webhooks.

Simple Relay decouples **ingestion acknowledgement** from **downstream execution**:
- Ingests the payload, validates cryptographic HMAC signatures, commits to durable storage, and answers the sender with `200 OK` in **under 2 milliseconds**.
- External senders immediately see a 100% healthy, lightning-fast endpoint.
- Simple Relay's background workers then forward payloads to your application at a safe, controlled pace.

### 3. Dead-Simple Deployment (One Self-Contained Binary)
Reliability shouldn't require managing an entire operations cluster. Simple Relay has zero external service dependencies—no separate databases to provision, no message brokers to monitor, and no complex queue workers to scale. 

Run it as a single binary on a Linux virtual machine or as a lightweight Docker container. It manages its own durable persistence, background worker pools, retry schedulers, and embedded management UI out of the box.

### 4. Client-Abort Aware Outbound Proxy
Standard reverse proxies continue blasting requests to external APIs even after the caller has disconnected. Simple Relay's synchronous proxy listens to incoming client connection state. If a client terminates the connection or times out, in-flight upstream requests and subsequent retry loops abort immediately to prevent wasted compute and upstream API rate limit exhaustion.

---

## High-Level Capabilities

| Capability | The Challenge | How Simple Relay Solves It |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Zero Data Loss** | Application restarts and deploy cycles drop in-flight requests. | Commits raw bytes to durable storage before returning `200 OK`. |
| **Ultra-Fast Inbound ACK** | Downstream processing causes timeouts from Stripe, Shopify, GitHub. | Decouples ingestion from execution; responds in `< 2ms`. |
| **Dead-Simple Deployment** | Message queues and worker clusters create heavy maintenance overhead. | Single self-contained binary with zero external services required. |
| **Smart Outbound Retries** | API rate limits (`429`) and server errors (`5xx`) disrupt operations. | Automatic retries with exponential backoff and randomized full jitter. |
| **Client Disconnect Awareness** | Dropped client requests waste third-party API quotas. | Aborts in-flight upstream requests immediately when callers drop. |
| **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)** | Exhausted retries vanish into server error logs. | Failed deliveries are safely preserved in the DLQ for one-click replay. |
| **Embedded Web UI** | Monitoring queue state requires setting up third-party dashboards. | Built-in browser UI with zero Node.js build pipeline or server processes. |

---

## Quickstart
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/quickstart

Get Simple Relay running and test your first reliable HTTP delivery in under 60 seconds.

## 1. Run Simple Relay

### Option A: Using Docker (Recommended)

Run the container in daemon mode, mounting a local folder for persistence:

```bash
docker run -d \
  --name simple-relay \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v $(pwd)/data:/data \
  ghcr.io/simple-relay/simple-relay:latest
```

### Option B: Standalone Binary

Download the compiled static binary from GitHub Releases or install via Go:

```bash
# Using Go 1.22+
go install github.com/simple-relay/simple-relay/cmd/relay@latest

# Run the relay
relay --listen :8080 --db-path ./relay.db
```

### Option C: Build from Source (Git Clone)

Clone the repository and compile the binary with standard Go:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/simple-relay/simple-relay.git
cd simple-relay

# Pure Go static build (no CGO required)
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o relay ./cmd/relay

# Run the compiled binary
./relay --listen :8080 --db-path ./relay.db
```

Verify that the relay is healthy:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/healthz
# {"status":"ok","version":"1.0.0"}
```

---

## 2. Ingest an Inbound Webhook

Simple Relay provides dedicated route endpoints under `/api/v1/webhook/:route`. Send a test payload:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/webhook/orders \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"order_id": "ord_99812", "amount": 4200, "currency": "usd"}'
```

Response:
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"queued","request_id":"01j9x0m1p00000000000000000"}
```

The raw bytes are durably persisted to storage before the `200 OK` response was sent. The delivery dispatcher is now forwarding this payload to your destination endpoint in the background.

---

## 3. Test Outbound Proxy with Smart Retries

Route an outgoing request to an upstream service through Simple Relay's synchronous retry proxy:

```bash
curl -i "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/proxy/sync?url=https://httpbin.org/status/200"
```

If the upstream server returns a `502 Bad Gateway` or `429 Too Many Requests`, Simple Relay automatically catches the failure and retries using exponential backoff with full jitter until the request succeeds or max attempts are reached.

---

## 4. Open the Embedded Dashboard

Open your browser and navigate to:

```text
http://localhost:8080/ui/
```

You can view:
- Inbound and outbound delivery logs.
- Attempt durations and latency graphs.
- Raw request and response payloads.
- Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) entries with one-click re-delivery.

---

## What's Next?

- Configure **[HMAC Signatures](/docs/stripe-github)** for Stripe or GitHub.
- Understand the **[Retries and Dead Letter Queue](/docs/retries-and-dlq)** mechanism.
- Inspect daemon health, queue backlog, and DLQ from your terminal using the **[CLI Reference](/docs/cli-reference)**.
- Check out the complete **[REST API Reference](/docs/api-reference)**.

## Inbound Webhooks
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/inbound-webhooks

Inbound webhooks are asynchronous push notifications from external third-party services (e.g., Stripe, Shopify, GitHub, Twilio). 

Because external services will often drop notifications or apply severe backoff penalties if your application is restarting, deploying, or undergoing heavy traffic spikes, handling webhooks directly inside application handlers creates significant risk of lost revenue and data inconsistencies.

## The Inbound Webhook Pipeline

Simple Relay operates as an autonomous edge buffer:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Sender["External Sender<br/>(Stripe, GitHub, etc.)"] -->|"HTTP POST (raw bytes)"| Ingest["Simple Relay Inbound"]
    
    subgraph Pipeline["Simple Relay Edge Engine"]
        Ingest --> Verify["1. Verify HMAC Signature"]
        Verify --> Commit["2. Commit Raw Bytes to Disk"]
        Commit --> Ack["3. Return HTTP 200 OK"]
        Commit --> Dispatcher["4. Background Worker Pool"]
    end
    
    Dispatcher -->|"Forward Payload"| Internal["Internal Application Destination"]
    Dispatcher -.->|"On Retry Exhaustion"| DLQ["Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)"]
```

---

## 1. The Durability Golden Rule: Persist Before ACK

> **Rule:** Never return HTTP `200 OK` or `202 Accepted` to the sender until the raw, unmodified byte payload is durably committed to storage.

When a webhook arrives at `/api/v1/webhook/:route_name`:
1. The raw payload stream is read into memory buffer.
2. If cryptographic verification is enabled, HMAC signature headers are validated against the raw byte buffer.
3. The raw byte sequence and headers are committed to disk.
4. Only upon successful flush does Simple Relay return `200 OK` with the tracking `request_id`.

If your internal application crashes, restarts, or runs out of database connections 5 seconds later, the webhook is completely safe on disk and will be delivered as soon as your service recovers.

---

## 2. Zero Byte Mutation & Signature Integrity

Many intermediate proxies or API gateways parse incoming JSON payloads into internal object representations and re-serialize them upon forwarding. 

Re-serialization alters whitespace, field order, and unicode escapes, which permanently breaks cryptographic HMAC signatures when downstream applications attempt secondary signature checks.

Simple Relay treats all inbound request bodies as immutable raw byte sequences (`[]byte`). Headers and body bytes forwarded downstream are bit-for-bit identical to what the external sender transmitted.

---

## 3. Configuring Inbound Routes

Inbound routes are registered dynamically via the REST API (`POST /api/v1/routes`) or configured in the embedded Web UI:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/routes \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "stripe-inbound",
    "type": "inbound",
    "mode": "async",
    "path": "/api/v1/webhook/stripe",
    "destination_url": "http://localhost:3000/api/webhooks/stripe",
    "signature_provider": "stripe",
    "signature_secret": "whsec_...",
    "max_attempts": 10,
    "timeout_ms": 10000,
    "retry_backoff_strategy": "exp"
  }'
```

When webhooks arrive, Simple Relay verifies the `Stripe-Signature` header, writes to disk, answers Stripe with `200 OK`, and forwards the verified payload to `http://localhost:3000/api/webhooks/stripe`.

---

## 4. Idempotency & Downstream Headers

Simple Relay guarantees **at-least-once delivery**. Transient network dropouts or backend timeouts can cause a delivery to be retried, which means your downstream application must handle duplicate requests safely.

To make idempotency effortless, Simple Relay automatically injects tracking headers into every request forwarded to your backend:

| Header | Example Value | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `X-Relay-Request-ID` | `01j9x0m1p00000000000000000` | Monotonic lowercase ULID uniquely identifying the persisted payload. Use this as your primary deduplication key. |
| `X-Relay-Attempt` | `1`, `2`, `3` | Incremental attempt counter. Indicates whether this is the first delivery or a subsequent retry. |
| `Idempotency-Key` | `idem_987123` | Preserved and forwarded downstream if sent by the caller or external webhook provider. |

### Backend Deduplication Pattern

In your downstream handler, simply store `X-Relay-Request-ID` in your database or cache (e.g. Redis `SET NX` or SQL unique constraint):

```javascript
// Express.js / Node.js
app.post('/api/webhooks/stripe', async (req, res) => {
  const relayId = req.headers['x-relay-request-id'];
  const attempt = req.headers['x-relay-attempt'];

  // Check if this delivery was already processed
  const alreadyProcessed = await db.processedWebhooks.findUnique({ where: { id: relayId } });
  if (alreadyProcessed) {
    return res.status(200).json({ status: 'already_processed' });
  }

  await processPayment(req.body);
  await db.processedWebhooks.create({ data: { id: relayId } });

  res.status(200).json({ status: 'success' });
});
```

---

- Learn about **[Retries and the Dead Letter Queue](/docs/retries-and-dlq)**.

## Outbound Proxy
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/outbound-proxy

Simple Relay provides two operational modes for handling outgoing HTTP requests to external third-party APIs and downstream services:

1. **Synchronous Transparent Proxy (`/api/v1/proxy/sync`)**
2. **Asynchronous Background Relay (`/api/v1/proxy/async`)**

---

## 1. Synchronous Transparent Proxy

Use the synchronous proxy when your application makes an outbound request to an external service and needs the response immediately to complete the current HTTP lifecycle, but wants resilience against transient network blips and rate limits.

### Request Flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    App["Your Backend"] -->|"HTTP Request"| Relay["Simple Relay Proxy"]
    Relay -->|"Call Upstream"| Upstream["Upstream API<br/>(OpenAI, Stripe, etc.)"]
    Upstream -->|"Response (2xx / non-retryable)"| Relay
    Relay -->|"Stream Back"| App
    
    Relay -.->|"Retries on 429 / 5xx"| Upstream
    App -.->|"Context Cancel on Disconnect"| Relay
```

### Usage Example

```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/proxy/sync?url=https://api.upstream.com/v1/charges" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sec_key_123" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"amount": 2000, "customer": "cus_123"}'
```

### Automatic 429 & 5xx Retries with `Retry-After` Support

When upstream responds with:
- `429 Too Many Requests`
- `502 Bad Gateway`, `503 Service Unavailable`, `504 Gateway Timeout`

Simple Relay intercepts the status code, inspects `Retry-After` headers (both integer seconds and RFC1123 HTTP dates), applies uniform full jitter, and retries the upstream request. Once upstream responds with `2xx` or non-retryable `4xx`, Simple Relay streams the response directly back to the caller.

### Client Disconnect Cancellation (Zero Wasted Compute)

> **Critical Safety Mechanism:** If your calling client closes its TCP connection, times out, or navigates away before Simple Relay finishes proxying, Simple Relay immediately triggers a Go context cancellation (`r.Context()`).

In-flight upstream requests are aborted instantaneously, and any scheduled retries are canceled. This prevents:
- Burning external API quotas when users have already left the page.
- Accumulating orphan worker goroutines during traffic spikes.

---

## 2. Asynchronous Background Relay

Use the asynchronous mode for fire-and-forget requests (sending emails, audit logs, analytics events, telemetry).

### Request Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    App["Your Backend"] -->|"POST /proxy/async"| Ingest["Simple Relay Ingest"]
    Ingest -->|"Commit to Storage"| Storage[("Durable Storage")]
    Storage -->|"Immediate ACK (< 2ms)"| ReturnAck["Return 202 Accepted"]
    ReturnAck --> App
    
    Storage --> Worker["Background Worker"]
    Worker -->|"Retries with Jitter"| Upstream["Upstream Service"]
```

### Usage Example

```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/proxy/async?url=https://api.resend.com/emails" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer re_123" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"from": "noreply@app.com", "to": "user@gmail.com", "subject": "Welcome!"}'
```

Response:
```http
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"accepted","request_id":"01j9x0z87q0000000000000000"}
```

The request returns in under 2 milliseconds. The payload is guaranteed to be delivered at-least-once according to your configured retry and backoff policy.

---

## Next Steps

- Explore how **[Retries and the Dead Letter Queue](/docs/retries-and-dlq)** handle persistent upstream outages.
- Read the **[Rate Limits and 429 Recipe](/docs/rate-limits-429)**.

## Retries & Dead Letter Queue
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/retries-and-dlq

When external networks or downstream microservices fail, naive retry strategies (such as immediate looping or fixed intervals) frequently trigger **Thundering Herd** disasters that overwhelm recovering services.

Simple Relay incorporates battle-tested exponential backoff, randomized full jitter, and a built-in Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).

---

## 1. Exponential Backoff with Full Jitter

Simple Relay implements the standard Full Jitter algorithm recommended by distributed systems engineering:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Full Jitter Exponential Backoff                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                  │
│   cap   = min( max_interval, initial_interval * 2^attempt )     │
│   sleep = random_between( 0, cap )                               │
│                                                                  │
│   Example (initial = 1s, max = 60s):                             │
│   • Attempt 1: random(0s .. 2s)   [avg: ~1.0s]                  │
│   • Attempt 2: random(0s .. 4s)   [avg: ~2.0s]                  │
│   • Attempt 3: random(0s .. 8s)   [avg: ~4.0s]                  │
│   • Attempt 4: random(0s .. 16s)  [avg: ~8.0s]                  │
│                                                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Why Full Jitter?

Without jitter, if an upstream API experiences a 10-second blip and 500 requests fail simultaneously, all 500 clients retry at exactly the same timestamps (2s, 4s, 8s), creating periodic traffic spikes that knock the recovering server offline again.

Full jitter scatters retry execution evenly across time, converting synchronized shockwaves into a smooth, manageable background trickle.

---

## 2. Retry Exhaustion and the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)

Every route or relay operation enforces bounded execution:
- `max_attempts` (default: `5`, configurable up to any positive integer)
- `initial_interval_ms` (default: `1000` ms)
- `max_interval_ms` (default: `60000` ms)
- `timeout_ms` (per-attempt HTTP timeout)

When all retry attempts are exhausted without receiving a successful response code (`2xx`), Simple Relay marks the delivery as `failed` and places it in the **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)**.

---

## 3. Replaying Deliveries from the DLQ

Simple Relay never discards failed payloads. You can inspect failures and trigger replays via the Web UI or REST API.

### Replay via Web UI

Navigate to `http://localhost:8080/ui/`, filter by status `FAILED` or navigate to the DLQ tab, select any delivery, inspect the error message and status code history, and click **Replay Delivery**.

### Replay a Single Delivery via REST API

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/requests/01j9x0m1p00000000000000000/replay
```

Response:
```json
{
  "status": "requeued",
  "request_id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000000",
  "attempt_count": 0
}
```

### Bulk Replay All Failed Deliveries

Once downstream services have recovered from an outage:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/dlq/replay \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"route": "stripe-inbound", "limit": 100}'
```

### Replay via `relay` CLI

For terminal workflows, scripts, or automated remediation:

```bash
# Replay a specific dead-lettered message
relay dlq replay 01j9x0m1p00000000000000000

# Bulk replay all failed DLQ messages without confirmation prompt
relay dlq replay-all -y
```

---

## Recipe: Stripe & GitHub Webhook HMAC
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/stripe-github

Simple Relay features native signature adapters for major webhook providers. It verifies incoming cryptographic signatures before saving the payload or sending acknowledgments, shielding your application from invalid or malicious requests.

---

## 1. Stripe Webhook Verification

Stripe secures webhooks using HMAC-SHA256 signatures passed in the `Stripe-Signature` header, which includes a UNIX timestamp `t` and signature `v1`.

### Route Configuration

Register the Stripe inbound route via `POST /api/v1/routes`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/routes \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "stripe-payments",
    "type": "inbound",
    "mode": "async",
    "path": "/api/v1/webhook/stripe",
    "destination_url": "http://app-backend:8000/webhooks/stripe",
    "signature_provider": "stripe",
    "signature_secret": "whsec_your_stripe_webhook_secret"
  }'
```

### How Simple Relay Verifies Stripe
1. Extracts `t` (timestamp) and `v1` (signature) from `Stripe-Signature`.
2. Validates that `|current_time - t| <= tolerance_seconds` (default 300s) to defeat replay attacks.
3. Computes `HMAC-SHA256(secret, t + "." + raw_body)`.
4. Executes constant-time equality check (`subtle.ConstantTimeCompare`) against `v1`.
5. If invalid, rejects with `401 Unauthorized` without touching your database or internal application.

---

## 2. GitHub Webhook Verification

GitHub transmits webhook signatures via the `X-Hub-Signature-256` header formatted as `sha256=<hex_digest>`.

### Route Configuration

Register the GitHub inbound route via `POST /api/v1/routes`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/routes \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "github-events",
    "type": "inbound",
    "mode": "async",
    "path": "/api/v1/webhook/github",
    "destination_url": "http://app-backend:8000/webhooks/github",
    "signature_provider": "github",
    "signature_secret": "your_github_webhook_secret"
  }'
```

### Verification Logic
Simple Relay calculates `HMAC-SHA256(secret, raw_body)` and matches it using constant-time comparison against the hex digest in `X-Hub-Signature-256`.

---

## 3. Generic HMAC-SHA256 Webhooks

For custom webhooks (e.g., Shopify, internal microservices), register a route using `hmac_sha256`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/routes \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "custom-events",
    "type": "inbound",
    "mode": "async",
    "path": "/api/v1/webhook/custom",
    "destination_url": "http://app-backend:8000/webhooks/custom",
    "signature_provider": "hmac_sha256",
    "signature_secret": "your_custom_secret"
  }'
```

---

## Testing Verification with `curl`

Generate a test HMAC-SHA256 signature and test your endpoint locally:

```bash
SECRET="whsec_test_secret_123"
BODY='{"event":"payment_intent.succeeded"}'
SIGNATURE=$(echo -n "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" | sed 's/^.* //')

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/webhook/custom \
  -H "X-Signature-SHA256: $SIGNATURE" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$BODY"
```

----------------------------------------

## Recipe: Handling 429 & Rate Limits
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/rate-limits-429

Modern SaaS APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Shopify, Twitter, Slack) strictly enforce rate limits. When your application exceeds quota, upstream returns:

```http
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
```

Failing to respect rate limits or immediately retrying in a tight loop can lead to temporary account suspension or permanent IP throttling.

---

## How Simple Relay Handles 429 Responses

When routing outbound traffic through `/api/v1/proxy/sync` or `/api/v1/proxy/async`:

1. **Automatic Status Detection:** Responses with status code `429` are flagged as transient retryable conditions.
2. **`Retry-After` Header Parsing:**
   - **Integer Seconds:** e.g., `Retry-After: 30` -> Simple Relay sleeps for 30 seconds (plus subtle uniform random jitter to avoid synchronicity).
   - **HTTP-Date:** e.g., `Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT` -> Simple Relay calculates the exact duration delta between current clock time and target timestamp.
3. **Fallback to Exponential Backoff:** If the upstream server returns `429` without a `Retry-After` header, Simple Relay automatically falls back to standard exponential backoff with full jitter.
4. **Context Respect:** If the synchronous caller terminates connection or hits its total timeout, Simple Relay cancels the upstream wait immediately.

---

## Route Configuration Example

When registering a route with sync retry proxying via `POST /api/v1/routes`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/routes \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "openai-proxy",
    "type": "outbound",
    "mode": "sync",
    "path": "/api/v1/relay/openai",
    "destination_url": "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
    "max_attempts": 8,
    "timeout_ms": 60000,
    "retry_backoff_strategy": "exp"
  }'
```

---

## Practical Example: Calling OpenAI Through Simple Relay

```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/proxy/sync?url=https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain HTTP idempotency in one sentence."}]
  }'
```

If OpenAI returns a `429` due to organization TPM/RPM limits, Simple Relay holds the connection, sleeps for the duration requested by OpenAI's `Retry-After` header, and retries seamlessly. Your backend application receives a clean `200 OK` as if the rate limit never happened.

----------------------------------------

## Recipe: Production Deployment
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/production-deploy

Because Simple Relay is packaged as a single self-contained binary, production deployment is straightforward and requires no complex orchestrators.

---

## 1. Docker Compose Setup

A standard production `docker-compose.yml` file:

```yaml
version: "3.8"

services:
  relay:
    image: ghcr.io/simple-relay/simple-relay:latest
    container_name: simple-relay
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - RELAY_LISTEN_ADDR=:8080
      - RELAY_DB_PATH=/data/relay.db
      - RELAY_WORKERS=8
      - RELAY_LOG_LEVEL=info
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data
    healthcheck:
      # Use relay for zero-dependency health checks (no curl required)
      test: ["CMD", "/usr/local/bin/relay", "health"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
```

> [!TIP] Zero-Dependency Probes
> In minimal container environments where `curl` or `wget` are absent, use `relay health` or `relay queue` to perform health checks and queue depth monitoring. See the **[CLI Reference](/docs/cli-reference)** for Docker and Kubernetes probe configurations.

Start the service:

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

---

## 2. Linux Systemd Service

For bare-metal servers or cloud virtual machines (EC2, Hetzner, DigitalOcean):

1. Place the compiled binary in `/usr/local/bin/relay`.
2. Create dedicated data directory:
   ```bash
   sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/simple-relay
   sudo useradd -r -s /bin/false simplerelay
   sudo chown -R simplerelay:simplerelay /var/lib/simple-relay
   ```
3. Create systemd unit at `/etc/systemd/system/simple-relay.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Simple Relay - Reliable HTTP Delivery Layer
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=simplerelay
Group=simplerelay
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/simple-relay
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/relay --listen :8080 --db-path /var/lib/simple-relay/relay.db
Restart=always
RestartSec=5s
LimitNOFILE=65535

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Enable and start:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now simple-relay
sudo systemctl status simple-relay
```

---

## 3. Continuous Streaming Backups with Litestream

For disaster recovery, pair Simple Relay with [Litestream](https://litestream.io/) to continuously stream point-in-time snapshots to AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, or any S3-compatible storage:

```yaml
# /etc/litestream.yml
dbs:
  - path: /var/lib/simple-relay/relay.db
    replicas:
      - url: s3://my-backup-bucket/simple-relay
        sync-interval: 1s
```

Run Litestream alongside Simple Relay:

```bash
litestream replicate -exec "/usr/local/bin/relay --listen :8080 --db-path /var/lib/simple-relay/relay.db"
```

If the host suffers catastrophic hardware failure, your entire database state can be restored instantly from S3 with zero data loss.

----------------------------------------

## Configuration Reference
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/configuration

Simple Relay adheres to the 12-factor application methodology. Configuration options are supplied via command-line flags and environment variables. Command-line flags take precedence over environment variables, which override default values.

---

## Server Daemon Settings Matrix

When running Simple Relay as a background daemon (`relay` or `relay serve`), the following flags and environment variables are supported. Both standard POSIX flags (`--host`) and single-dash flags (`-host`) are accepted:

| CLI Flag | Environment Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `--host`, `-host` | `RELAY_HOST` | `0.0.0.0` | Server host address. |
| `--port`, `-port` | `RELAY_PORT` (or `PORT`) | `8080` | Server HTTP port. |
| `--db`, `-db` | `RELAY_DB_PATH` | `relay.db` | Path to persistent SQLite database file. |
| `--log-level`, `-log-level` | `RELAY_LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | Logging verbosity: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`. |
| `--workers`, `-workers` | `RELAY_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` | `20` | Outbound worker pool concurrency. |
| `--dispatcher-buffer`, `-dispatcher-buffer` | `RELAY_DISPATCHER_BUFFER` | `0` (dynamic: `2 * workers`) | Dispatcher jobs channel buffer capacity. |
| `--dispatcher-poll-ms`, `-dispatcher-poll-ms` | `RELAY_DISPATCHER_POLL_MS` | `500` | Dispatcher polling interval in milliseconds. |
| `--cleaner-interval`, `-cleaner-interval` | `RELAY_CLEANER_INTERVAL` | `1h` | Storage retention cleaner execution interval. |
| `--drain-timeout`, `-drain-timeout` | `RELAY_DRAIN_TIMEOUT` | `30s` | Graceful shutdown drain timeout. |
| — | `RELAY_RETENTION_SUCCESS_DAYS` | `7` | Retention period in days for successfully delivered records. |
| — | `RELAY_RETENTION_FAILED_DAYS` | `30` | Retention period in days for failed/dead-lettered records. |
| — | `RELAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `""` | Optional admin authentication secret for API endpoints. |
| — | `RELAY_BATCH_SIZE` | `50` | Maximum requests grouped per SQLite WAL write transaction. |
| — | `RELAY_BATCH_TIMEOUT_MS` | `10` | Maximum batch linger duration before flushing to SQLite. |

---

## CLI Subcommands Settings Matrix

When executing operator subcommands (`relay health`, `relay queue`, `relay dlq`), the following global persistent flags and environment variables configure remote daemon connectivity and output formatting:

| CLI Flag | Environment Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `-s, --server` | `RELAY_SERVER_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:8080` | Target Simple Relay daemon HTTP/HTTPS address. |
| `-k, --api-key` | `RELAY_API_KEY` | `""` | Admin API key for protected management endpoints. |
| `-o, --output` | `RELAY_OUTPUT` | `table` | Output format: `table` (human-readable) or `json` (scripting). |
| `--timeout` | `RELAY_TIMEOUT` | `10s` | HTTP client request timeout duration. |

> [!TIP] Detailed Subcommand Documentation
> For subcommand recipes, interactive confirmation overrides, and orchestration probe configurations, see the **[CLI Reference](/docs/cli-reference)**.

---

## Dynamic Route Configuration

Routes in Simple Relay are managed dynamically at runtime via the REST API (`/api/v1/routes`) or the embedded Web UI, avoiding static configuration files and service restarts. Routes are persisted in SQLite and hot-reloaded into memory.

### Route Creation Example (`POST /api/v1/routes`)

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/routes \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "stripe-inbound",
    "type": "inbound",
    "mode": "async",
    "path": "/api/v1/webhook/stripe",
    "destination_url": "http://internal-backend:8000/webhooks/stripe",
    "signature_provider": "stripe",
    "signature_secret": "whsec_...",
    "max_attempts": 10,
    "timeout_ms": 15000,
    "retry_backoff_strategy": "exp"
  }'
```

----------------------------------------

## REST API Reference
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/api-reference

Simple Relay exposes a lightweight, high-performance REST API for ingesting webhooks, routing proxies, inspecting deliveries, replaying dead-lettered requests, and managing administrative credentials.

---

## 1. Authentication & Security Model

Simple Relay implements a dual authentication architecture supporting both programmatic service-to-service automation and interactive browser-based Web UI sessions.

### Operational Modes

- **Dev Mode (`RELAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=""`):**
  When `RELAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is empty or unset (default), all management endpoints are open without authentication. This mode provides friction-free local development and zero-configuration testing.
- **Protected Mode (`RELAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD="<secret>"`):**
  When `RELAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is set, all management, telemetry, and inspection endpoints require authentication. Public ingestion and health probe endpoints remain accessible.

### Dual Authentication Credentials

When Protected Mode is active, authenticate via either mechanism:

1. **API Key (Service-to-Service):**
   Provide a valid API key in incoming HTTP headers:
   ```http
   X-API-Key: sr_live_a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90
   ```
   Or via standard Bearer authorization:
   ```http
   Authorization: Bearer sr_live_a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90
   ```
2. **Admin Session Cookie (Web UI):**
   Obtained by authenticating via `POST /api/v1/auth/login`. Sets an HTTP-only `relay_session` cookie valid for 24 hours.

### Endpoint Access Matrix

| Method | Endpoint | Authentication | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/webhook/:route_name` | Public (Provider Signature) | Durable webhook ingestion into SQLite WAL |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/jobs/:route_name` | Public | Asynchronous delivery job enqueue |
| `ANY` | `/api/v1/relay/:route_name` | Public | Synchronous proxy with automatic retries |
| `GET` | `/healthz` | Public | System health check and liveness probe |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/auth/status` | Public | Check auth requirement and active session |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/auth/login` | Public (Rate-limited) | Authenticate admin password and obtain session |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/auth/logout` | Public | Invalidate admin session and clear cookie |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/routes` | Protected | List all configured routes |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/routes` | Protected | Create and hot-reload a new route |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/routes/:id` | Protected | Retrieve route configuration by ID |
| `PUT` | `/api/v1/routes/:id` | Protected | Update route configuration by ID |
| `DELETE` | `/api/v1/routes/:id` | Protected | Delete route configuration by ID |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/requests` | Protected | List requests with pagination and filters |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/requests/:id` | Protected | Inspect delivery record, payload, and attempts |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/jobs/:job_id` | Protected | Inspect asynchronous job status and attempts |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/queue/stats` | Protected | Real-time queue metrics and backlog telemetry |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/dlq` | Protected | List dead-lettered requests |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/dlq/:request_id/replay` | Protected | Requeue an individual dead-lettered request |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/dlq/replay-all` | Protected | Bulk requeue dead-lettered requests |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/api-keys` | Protected | Generate a new API key |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/api-keys` | Protected | List existing API keys (masked) |
| `DELETE` | `/api/v1/api-keys/:id` | Protected | Revoke an API key |

---

## 2. Public Ingress & Proxy Endpoints

### `POST /api/v1/webhook/:route_name`
Ingests an inbound webhook, verifies cryptographic signatures (if configured on the route), durably commits raw payload bytes to SQLite WAL storage, and enqueues background delivery. Also supports `PUT` and `PATCH`.

- **Headers:**
  - Provider signature headers (e.g. `Stripe-Signature`, `X-Hub-Signature-256`, etc.).
  - `X-Relay-Request-ID` *(optional)*: Custom tracking ULID/UUID. Simple Relay generates a monotonic ULID if omitted.
- **Status Codes:**
  - `200 OK`: Payload durably persisted in SQLite storage.
  - `400 Bad Request`: Route not configured for inbound mode or invalid JSON body.
  - `401 Unauthorized`: Provider signature verification or header rule failed.
  - `404 Not Found`: Route name not found.
  - `413 Payload Too Large`: Payload exceeds body limit (default: 10MB).
  - `500 Internal Server Error`: SQLite WAL write failure.
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "relay_id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000000",
    "status": "persisted"
  }
  ```

### `POST /api/v1/jobs/:route_name`
Fire-and-forget asynchronous job ingestion. Persists the request to SQLite WAL storage and schedules immediate delivery by background dispatcher workers.

- **Status Code:** `202 Accepted`
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "job_id": "01j9x0z87q00000000000000000",
    "status": "queued"
  }
  ```

### `ANY /api/v1/relay/:route_name`
Synchronous outbound proxy for routes configured with `mode: "sync"`. Transparently forwards HTTP method, headers, and request body to the configured destination URL.

- **Automatic Retries:** Automatically retries transient upstream failures (`429 Too Many Requests`, `502`, `503`, `504`) with exponential backoff and randomized full jitter.
- **Client Disconnect Cancellation:** Cancels in-flight upstream execution immediately if the calling client closes the connection (`r.Context()`), eliminating wasted compute and downstream quota consumption.
- **Returns:** Transparent upstream status code, response headers, and body.

---

## 3. Authentication & Sessions (Public)

### `GET /api/v1/auth/status`
Checks whether server authentication is required and if the current client is authenticated.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "auth_required": true,
    "authenticated": false
  }
  ```

### `POST /api/v1/auth/login`
Authenticates an administrator with the configured `RELAY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and issues an HTTP-only session cookie.

- **Rate Limiting:** Enforces brute-force lockout (max 5 failed attempts within 5 minutes per IP). Returns `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header when locked.
- **Request Body:**
  ```json
  {
    "password": "your-admin-password"
  }
  ```
- **Response Format (`200 OK`):**
  - Sets `relay_session` cookie (valid 24 hours, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` when HTTPS).
  ```json
  {
    "status": "authenticated"
  }
  ```

### `POST /api/v1/auth/logout`
Invalidates the current session token in memory and clears the `relay_session` cookie.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "status": "logged_out"
  }
  ```

---

## 4. Route Management (Protected)

Routes configure forwarding destinations, retry backoff strategies, timeouts, and cryptographic signature verification. Modifications hot-reload into memory immediately without service restarts.

### `GET /api/v1/routes`
Lists all configured routes.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  [
    {
      "id": "01j9x0r7000000000000000000",
      "name": "stripe-inbound",
      "type": "inbound",
      "mode": "async",
      "path": "/api/v1/webhook/stripe",
      "destination_url": "https://api.internal.com/webhooks/stripe",
      "signature_provider": "stripe",
      "signature_secret": "whsec_...",
      "max_attempts": 5,
      "timeout_ms": 10000,
      "retry_backoff_strategy": "exp",
      "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:00:00Z",
      "updated_at": "2026-10-15T01:00:00Z"
    }
  ]
  ```

### `POST /api/v1/routes`
Creates and registers a new routing configuration.

- **Request Body:**
  ```json
  {
    "name": "github-webhook",
    "type": "inbound",
    "mode": "async",
    "path": "/api/v1/webhook/github",
    "destination_url": "https://api.internal.com/webhooks/github",
    "signature_provider": "github",
    "signature_secret": "secret123",
    "max_attempts": 5,
    "timeout_ms": 10000,
    "retry_backoff_strategy": "exp"
  }
  ```
- **Status Code:** `201 Created`

### `GET /api/v1/routes/:id`
Retrieves a single route configuration by ULID.

### `PUT /api/v1/routes/:id`
Updates an existing route configuration by ULID and hot-reloads the internal registry.

### `DELETE /api/v1/routes/:id`
Deletes a route configuration by ULID.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "status": "deleted"
  }
  ```

---

## 5. Delivery & Request Inspection (Protected)

### `GET /api/v1/requests`
List recorded delivery requests with pagination and status filters.

- **Query Parameters:**
  - `status`: Filter by status (`pending`, `delivering`, `delivered`, `failed`).
  - `route_id`: Filter by route ULID.
  - `search`: Filter by text contained in destination URL.
  - `limit`: Number of records (default: `50`, max: `100`).
  - `offset`: Pagination offset (default: `0`).
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "items": [
      {
        "id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
        "route_id": "01j9x0r7000000000000000000",
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "https://api.internal.com/webhooks/stripe",
        "status": "delivered",
        "attempts_count": 2,
        "last_error": null,
        "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:00Z",
        "updated_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:03Z"
      }
    ],
    "total": 1,
    "limit": 50,
    "offset": 0
  }
  ```

### `GET /api/v1/requests/:id`
Fetch single delivery record including headers, raw payload body, and historical attempt logs.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
    "route_id": "01j9x0r7000000000000000000",
    "method": "POST",
    "url": "https://api.internal.com/webhooks/stripe",
    "headers": {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Stripe-Signature": "t=1728950000,v1=..."
    },
    "body": "{\"id\":\"evt_123\",\"type\":\"payment_intent.succeeded\"}",
    "status": "delivered",
    "attempts_count": 2,
    "last_error": null,
    "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:00Z",
    "updated_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:03Z",
    "attempts": [
      {
        "id": "01j9x0m2000000000000000001",
        "request_id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
        "attempt_number": 1,
        "status_code": 503,
        "duration_ms": 42,
        "error_message": "upstream service unavailable",
        "attempted_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:01Z"
      },
      {
        "id": "01j9x0m3000000000000000002",
        "request_id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
        "attempt_number": 2,
        "status_code": 200,
        "duration_ms": 18,
        "error_message": null,
        "attempted_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:03Z"
      }
    ]
  }
  ```

### `GET /api/v1/jobs/:job_id`
Inspect status, retry scheduling, and execution history for an asynchronous background job.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "id": "01j9x0z87q00000000000000000",
    "route_id": "01j9x0r7000000000000000000",
    "method": "POST",
    "url": "https://api.internal.com/jobs/process",
    "status": "pending",
    "attempts_count": 0,
    "next_attempt_at": "2026-10-15T01:15:00Z",
    "last_error": null,
    "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:15:00Z",
    "updated_at": "2026-10-15T01:15:00Z",
    "attempts": []
  }
  ```

---

## 6. Queue Telemetry (Protected)

### `GET /api/v1/queue/stats`
Returns real-time queue depth and active worker processing metrics.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "pending": 8,
    "in_flight": 3,
    "queue_depth": 11,
    "status": "HEALTHY"
  }
  ```

> [!NOTE] Backlog Threshold
> When total `queue_depth` (`pending + in_flight`) reaches or exceeds **1,000**, the `status` field switches from `HEALTHY` to `BACKLOG`. This provides an immediate zero-parsing signal for autoscaling policies and system alerts.

---

## 7. Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) Management (Protected)

When a delivery exhausts its maximum retry attempts without receiving a 2xx response, it is permanently marked as `failed` and preserved in the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).

### `GET /api/v1/dlq`
Lists dead-lettered requests awaiting manual triage or automated replay.

- **Query Parameters:**
  - `route_name`: Optional filter by route name.
  - `limit`: Number of records (default: `50`, max: `500`).
  - `offset`: Pagination offset (default: `0`).
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "items": [
      {
        "id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
        "route_id": "01j9x0r7000000000000000000",
        "method": "POST",
        "url": "https://api.internal.com/webhooks/stripe",
        "status": "dlq",
        "attempts_count": 5,
        "last_error": "connection refused",
        "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:10:00Z",
        "updated_at": "2026-10-15T01:12:30Z"
      }
    ],
    "total": 1,
    "limit": 50,
    "offset": 0
  }
  ```

### `POST /api/v1/dlq/:request_id/replay`
Requeues an individual failed delivery for immediate retry and wakes the dispatcher worker pool immediately.

- **Status Codes:** `200 OK` on replay; `404 Not Found` if ID does not exist; `409 Conflict` if request is not in DLQ status.
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "id": "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
    "status": "pending",
    "replayed": true,
    "replayed_at": "2026-10-15T01:20:00Z"
  }
  ```

### `POST /api/v1/dlq/replay-all`
Bulk requeues dead-lettered deliveries matching filter criteria and immediately triggers delivery workers.

- **Request Body (Optional):**
  ```json
  {
    "route_name": "stripe-inbound",
    "limit": 100
  }
  ```
  *(Default limit: `100`, max: `1000` to prevent downstream thundering herd shockwaves).*
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "replayed_count": 14,
    "request_ids": [
      "01j9x0m1p00000000000000001",
      "01j9x0m1p00000000000000002"
    ]
  }
  ```

---

## 8. API Key Management (Protected)

Administrative API keys allow secure service-to-service communication with Simple Relay management endpoints without managing browser session cookies.

### `POST /api/v1/api-keys`
Generates a new administrative API key. Returns the raw secret token once.

- **Request Body:**
  ```json
  {
    "name": "worker-ci"
  }
  ```
- **Status Code:** `201 Created`
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "id": "01j9x0k8000000000000000001",
    "name": "worker-ci",
    "key": "sr_live_a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90a1b2c3d4e5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f90",
    "masked_key": "sr_live_a1b*****8f90",
    "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:30:00Z"
  }
  ```

> [!WARNING] Raw Token Exposure
> The unmasked `key` (`sr_live_...`) is returned **only once** upon generation. Simple Relay hashes the token with SHA-256 before persisting to SQLite and never stores the plaintext key. Store the raw key securely in your environment variables or secrets vault.

### `GET /api/v1/api-keys`
Lists all active and revoked API keys with metadata and masked keys.

- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  [
    {
      "id": "01j9x0k8000000000000000001",
      "name": "worker-ci",
      "masked_key": "sr_live_a1b*****8f90",
      "created_at": "2026-10-15T01:30:00Z",
      "revoked_at": null
    }
  ]
  ```

### `DELETE /api/v1/api-keys/:id`
Immediately revokes an active API key by ULID. Revoked keys cannot be used for authentication.

- **Status Code:** `200 OK` on revocation; `404 Not Found` if already revoked or non-existent.
- **Response Format:**
  ```json
  {
    "id": "01j9x0k8000000000000000001",
    "status": "revoked"
  }
  ```

---

## 9. System & Health (Public)

### `GET /healthz`
Standard operational liveness probe returning HTTP `200 OK` and system timestamp.

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-15T01:25:00Z"
}
```

----------------------------------------

## Embedded Web UI
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/embedded-ui

Simple Relay packages an administrative Web UI directly inside the Go binary via `go:embed`. It requires zero external Node.js dependencies or separate frontend server processes.

Access the dashboard at:

```text
http://localhost:8080/ui/
```

---

## Key Features of the Dashboard

### 1. Real-time Delivery Log
Inspect all inbound webhooks and outbound proxy calls:
- Chronologically sorted by monotonic ULID timestamp.
- Filter by status (`QUEUED`, `DELIVERING`, `DELIVERED`, `FAILED`).
- Visual latency badges showing duration per delivery attempt.

### 2. Payload & Header Inspector
Clicking any request opens an inspection modal showing:
- Bit-for-bit raw incoming request headers and payload body.
- Forwarded destination URL.
- Upstream response headers and response body (truncated to safe size limits).

### 3. Attempt History & Error Traces
When upstream services fail, inspect:
- Number of attempts made.
- Exact backoff delay calculated with full jitter.
- Error messages (e.g. connection refused, TLS handshake timeout, 502 Bad Gateway).

### 4. One-Click Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) Replay
Any delivery in the `FAILED` state features an interactive **Replay** button. Click to requeue the message instantly without re-sending from the external webhook provider.

----------------------------------------

## CLI Reference
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/cli-reference

Operator inspection tooling is embedded directly into the primary `relay` binary. Running `relay` without subcommands (or `relay serve`) launches the reliability daemon; running subcommands (`health`, `status`, `queue`, `dlq`) executes operator inspection and triage tasks from the terminal without browser access.

Rather than opening or locking the SQLite database directly, CLI subcommands interact exclusively with Simple Relay's REST API over HTTP/HTTPS. This architecture prevents SQLite lock contention (`SQLITE_BUSY`), eliminates shared memory overhead, and allows operators to inspect or manage remote daemons across networks or from lightweight container environments.

---

## 1. Installation & Build

Simple Relay is distributed as a single static binary with CGO disabled:

### Compile from Source

```bash
# Build the unified static binary
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o relay ./cmd/relay
```

### Install via Go Toolchain

```bash
go install github.com/simple-relay/simple-relay/cmd/relay@latest
```

---

## 2. Global Flags & Environment Variables

All `relay` CLI subcommands accept global flags and support configuration through environment variables:

| CLI Flag | Environment Variable | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `-s, --server` | `RELAY_SERVER_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:8080` | Simple Relay daemon base URL. |
| `-k, --api-key` | `RELAY_API_KEY` | `""` | Admin API key for authenticated endpoints. |
| `-o, --output` | `RELAY_OUTPUT` | `table` | Output format: `table` (human-readable) or `json` (scripting). |
| `--timeout` | `RELAY_TIMEOUT` | `10s` | HTTP request client timeout duration (e.g., `5s`, `30s`). |

---

## 3. Core Commands & Usage

### 3.1 Daemon Health & Latency (`health` / `status`)

Probes the `/healthz` endpoint, measures end-to-end round-trip network latency, and returns standardized POSIX exit codes suitable for orchestration probes:

```bash
relay health
# Or alias
relay status
```

#### Example Output (Table):
```
STATUS   LATENCY   SERVER TIME                   URL
OK       0.45ms    2026-10-15T01:25:00.000000Z   http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

#### Example Output (JSON):
```bash
relay health -o json
```
```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "latency_ms": 0,
  "timestamp": "2026-10-15T01:25:00.000000Z",
  "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
}
```

#### Exit Codes:

| Exit Code | Condition | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `0` | **Healthy** | Daemon returned HTTP 200 and operational status `ok`. |
| `1` | **Unreachable** | Connection refused, DNS failure, or client timeout. |
| `2` | **Degraded** | Daemon reachable but reported unhealthy or degraded state. |

---

### 3.2 Queue Depth & Backlog Monitoring (`queue`)

Inspects the number of pending and active in-flight delivery jobs across background dispatcher workers:

```bash
relay queue
```

#### Example Output (Table):
```
QUEUE DEPTH   PENDING   IN-FLIGHT   STATUS
14            10        4           HEALTHY
```

#### Example Output (JSON):
```bash
relay queue -o json
```
```json
{
  "queue_depth": 14,
  "pending": 10,
  "in_flight": 4,
  "status": "HEALTHY"
}
```

> [!NOTE] Backlog Alerting
> If total queue depth (`pending + in_flight`) reaches or exceeds **1,000 requests**, `relay queue` marks status as `BACKLOG` and exits with **code 2**. This enables automated autoscaling or alert triggering in monitoring pipelines without custom parsing scripts.

---

### 3.3 Dead Letter Queue Inspection (`dlq`)

Inspect and triage dead-lettered requests that have exhausted all configured retry attempts.

#### List DLQ Records

```bash
relay dlq list
relay dlq list --limit 100
```

Example Output:
```
REQUEST ID                    ROUTE           ATTEMPTS   FAILED AT             LAST ERROR
01j9x0m1p00000000000000001   stripe-inbound  5          2026-10-15 01:12:04   upstream returned HTTP 500 Internal Server...
01j9x0z87q00000000000000002   github-webhook  5          2026-10-15 01:14:22   connection reset by peer
```

#### Inspect Detailed Record & Attempt Audit Trail

```bash
relay dlq inspect 01j9x0m1p00000000000000001
```

Example Output:
```
Request ID:    01j9x0m1p00000000000000001
Route ID:      stripe-inbound
Method:        POST
Destination:   http://internal-backend:8000/webhooks/stripe
Status:        FAILED
Created At:    2026-10-15T01:10:00Z
Last Error:    upstream returned HTTP 500 Internal Server Error

Attempt History:
#   ATTEMPTED AT          STATUS CODE   DURATION   ERROR
1   2026-10-15 01:10:01   500           23ms       upstream returned HTTP 500
2   2026-10-15 01:10:03   500           19ms       upstream returned HTTP 500
3   2026-10-15 01:10:07   500           21ms       upstream returned HTTP 500
4   2026-10-15 01:10:15   500           25ms       upstream returned HTTP 500
5   2026-10-15 01:10:31   500           20ms       upstream returned HTTP 500
```

---

### 3.4 Replaying DLQ Messages (`dlq replay`)

#### Replay Single Request

Requeues a specific dead-lettered request for immediate retry:

```bash
relay dlq replay 01j9x0m1p00000000000000001
```

```
Successfully requeued request 01j9x0m1p00000000000000001 for delivery.
```

#### Replay All Failed Requests (Bulk Replay)

Requeues all messages currently in the DLQ. When run in an interactive terminal, `relay` prompts for confirmation:

```bash
relay dlq replay-all
# Found 42 items in DLQ. Requeue all for delivery? [y/N]: y
# Successfully requeued 42 DLQ requests for delivery.
```

In CI/CD, cron jobs, or headless deployment scripts, pass `--yes` (`-y`) to bypass confirmation:

```bash
relay dlq replay-all -y
```

---

## 4. Headless & Container Probe Recipes

Because Simple Relay compiles into a single, static CGO-free binary, container images only need the `relay` binary for both serving traffic and executing health/readiness probes (no `curl`, `wget`, or `jq` needed).

### Docker Container Health Check

Add to your `Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["/usr/local/bin/relay", "health"]
```

### Kubernetes Probes

Configure Kubernetes `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` directly in your Pod manifest:

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
    - name: relay
      image: simple-relay:latest
      livenessProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - /usr/local/bin/relay
            - health
        initialDelaySeconds: 3
        periodSeconds: 10
        timeoutSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 3
      readinessProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - /usr/local/bin/relay
            - queue
        initialDelaySeconds: 2
        periodSeconds: 5
        timeoutSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 2
```

> [!TIP] Zero-Downtime Backlog Protection
> The `readinessProbe` using `relay queue` automatically fails (exit code 2) if queue depth exceeds 1,000 jobs, prompting Kubernetes Service routing to temporarily stop sending new inbound requests to an overloaded replica until its queue drains.

----------------------------------------

## Benchmarks & Performance
Source: https://simplerelay.dev/docs/benchmarks

Simple Relay is engineered in pure Go to deliver maximum reliability with a near-zero memory footprint.

Unlike in-memory queues that acknowledge receipt before committing to disk, Simple Relay enforces the **Durability Golden Rule**: an inbound webhook is never acknowledged with HTTP `200 OK` until its raw byte payload is safely flushed to persistent storage.

Below are the official benchmark measurements conducted against Release `v0.3.0`.

These are Simple Relay measurements, not a head-to-head comparison with another webhook product. They show request acknowledgement and durable ingestion performance under the listed test conditions. Results depend on hardware, storage, network, configuration, and workload. Use the reproduction steps below to run the same workload in your own environment before comparing systems.

---

## 1. Concurrency & Ingestion Throughput

Tests were executed using [`bombardier`](https://github.com/codesenberg/bombardier) using realistic 1.5 KB JSON webhook payloads (containing customer IDs, line items, timestamps, and nested metadata).

### Ingestion Performance Matrix (1,000 Requests / Tier)

| Concurrency | Ingest Throughput | Avg Latency | p50 Latency | p90 Latency | p95 Latency | p99 Latency | Error Rate |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **10** | **848 req/s** | 11.4 ms | 10.1 ms | 10.8 ms | 37.8 ms | 38.8 ms | **0.00%** |
| **50** | **6,280 req/s** | 7.4 ms | **4.1 ms** | 8.5 ms | 33.8 ms | 43.0 ms | **0.00%** |
| **100** | **8,708 req/s** | 12.2 ms | **5.8 ms** | 36.4 ms | 41.8 ms | **42.8 ms** | **0.00%** |

---

## 2. Sustained 10-Second Saturation Run

To test memory stability, garbage collection pauses, and CPU efficiency under sustained saturation, Simple Relay was bombarded for 10 seconds continuously at 100 concurrent connections:

- **Total Requests Handled:** **100,622 requests**
- **Average Ingest Throughput:** **10,058 req/s**
- **Median Latency (p50):** **5.65 ms**
- **p95 Latency:** **35.81 ms**
- **p99 Latency:** **39.73 ms**
- **Failed Requests:** **0** (100% durable persistence confirmed)

---

## 3. Resource Footprint & RAM Profile

Measurements sampled directly via `docker stats` during idle, peak load, and post-load background drain phases:

| State | CPU Usage | RAM Usage | RAM % of Host | Description |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Idle** | `< 0.5%` | **4.2 MiB** | `~0.01%` | Baseline idle memory |
| **Peak Load (10,000 RPS)** | `~145%` | **24.0 – 26.1 MiB** | `~0.04%` | Sustained 10k req/s using ~1.45 CPU cores |
| **Post-Load (Drain Phase)** | `~2.5%` | **21.1 MiB** | `~0.03%` | Asynchronous worker pool processing |

> **Key Takeaway:** Even under a sustained bombardment of 10,000 requests per second, Simple Relay stays well under **26 MB of RAM**, making it viable to deploy on the smallest $5/month cloud instances without memory pressure.

---

## 4. How to Reproduce

You can reproduce these benchmarks on your own machine using the test runner in the Simple Relay repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/simple-relay/simple-relay.git
cd simple-relay

# Run automated container benchmark
./scripts/benchmark.sh

# Run custom volume test (5,000 requests, 100 concurrency)
NUM_REQUESTS=5000 CONCURRENCY_LIST="10 50 100" ./scripts/benchmark.sh
```
